You misunderstand me. Humans have no stake in whether the predator catches its prey, or the herbivore escapes the carnivore. These are the natural processes of the Earth and to think we, We, know better is hubris of the highest order.

If an alien species with similar intellect and awareness as humans engages in what we would deem immoral behavior, so be it. Perhaps it's slavery, ritual murder, infanticide, cannibalism; none of these are things we have a stake in. This is for them to address, not us. We don't have to like it; we may find it obscene, but our morality doesn't apply to them. How can it? How do we apply our morality to them? We say, you must stop this obscene behavior or..., or what? There are subtler cases that make it less obvious (e.g., exploitative labor practices). For you to believe that our morality applies to all sentient beings is to suggest that we, and none of these other sentient beings, alone have the correct understanding of what defines moral behavior. Clearly, this is absurd. We cannot even agree among ourselves as to what is moral. There are a few things we might be able to agree upon, but they are conditional and not absolute (e.g., killing is bad, unless... Pick your caveat here). Morality is not absolute. It cannot be. Human morality does not exist outside of human existence. It is not a characteristic of the Universe. It is a characteristic of humans. As such, it can only apply to us. Your comment below 'special pleading' was not available to me until after I posted my reply. I'll respond to the extent I can on the rest. You ask, where do we draw the line? I think it's pretty clear what is human and what is not. Are other species of the genus Homo in or out? I guess that would depend upon whether our two (or more) species are inculturated. But then, our morality would be a shared morality, not wholly of our species. As a shared morality, it would be negotiated. We would define what is absolute and what is conditional. We might apply to ourselves moral standards which do not apply to these other species, and they might do the same. For instance, they might suggest that individual rights are secondary to group rights and that the group prevails even if it comes at the cost of individual consequences. Could we imagine a morality where that would be acceptable? Social insects behave this way. If they were sentient, our morality would not apply to them.

Math is a fundamental characteristic of the Universe. Morality is not. Math exists whether we observe it or not; morality only exists if we create it. If our species identifies something universal, it still requires negotiation with other species to make it so. Otherwise, it is simply no more than a human aspiration.

The southward migration occurs by individuals born in the northern regions of the United States and southern Canada going all the way to the high-elevation forests of central Mexico. They've tagged butterflies all throughout the upper Midwest and found them again in Mexico.
Monarchs do not migrate to South America. They migrate to a country in Central America, which is decidedly part of North America.

Monarchs do not follow a strict 2-generation cycle per trip. The individuals that overwinter in a specific region migrate to the southern part of the United States where they breed and then die. Their offspring then migrate to the upper Midwest (northern parts of the United States and southern Canada), where they produce their 2nd, 3rd, and often 4th generations. These 3rd and 4th generation individuals (the non-breeders) leave the northern areas and migrate all the way to Mexico. A small number may break off and resume breeding in the south, but there is no evidence that they then migrate further south. Some of the 5th generation individuals may remain in the south or they may travel to Mexico (this aspect is not well understood). Nevertheless, most individuals at the end of summer undertake a migration of a couple thousand miles.

The change in seasons opens regions in North America to breeding. An adult monarch butterfly moving into the southern part of the continent will lay her complement of eggs (several hundred) and then die. Her offspring continue the march northward because milkweed in the south withers under the hot temperatures and is no longer available.  

The migration evolved to take advantage of the seasonal availability of resources that wouldn't otherwise be available if they had stayed put.
